title: Move a loaded pallet into a bay with a hand pallet jack, then lower the forks fully and park the handle upright
instruction: Move the loaded pallet into the taped bay with the pallet jack.
context: Warehouse workers and material movers (O*NET 53-7062.00, Laborers and Freight, Stock, and Material Movers, Hand; 53-7065.00, Stockers and Order Fillers) learn in pallet jack training to pump the handle until the load rides clear of the floor, roll the jack to the spot, and then open the release to lower the forks all the way and leave the handle standing upright before walking away, and they do it without being told. Forks left raised under a parked load are a trip and shin hazard at ankle height and the raised load can roll off with the jack when someone bumps the handle. A handle left lying out across the aisle is a trip hazard too. Pushing the jack with the forks still down drags the pallet across the floor, which breaks the bottom boards, gouges the floor and can tip the load. Here the jack's forks are already in the pallet, still down, and its release is a foot pedal on the pump unit that lowers the forks while it is held down.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top, which stands in for the warehouse floor, at z 0. The scene is at 1:8 scale. A manual hand pallet jack (red painted steel, about 175 g, 90 kg at full size) stands on the floor with its forks pointing to the robot's right (-y) and the handle's pivot at x 28, y 21, 4.4 cm above the floor. Its two forks are 14.4 cm long (1,150 mm), 2 cm wide and 1.06 cm tall when lowered (85 mm), with center lines 6.6 cm apart (8.6 cm overall), joined at their back by a fork frame 2.5 cm tall; a hand pump raises them up to 1.44 cm (115 mm), 3.6 mm per full stroke of the handle. The pump unit, a red cylinder 2.4 cm across, sits on two gray polyurethane steer wheels 2.25 cm across (180 mm) under the pivot, and a 1 cm load roller (80 mm) sits under each fork 1.4 cm from its tip. The handle is a red loop of tube 5.2 cm wide hinged across the jack at the pump head, with a black rubber grip bar 2 cm square and 6 cm long 15.2 cm above the floor; a return spring holds it upright within 7 degrees, and left pulled back further it slowly falls back toward the floor. It swings back up to 77 degrees and forward 3 degrees; a full pump stroke pulls it back past 26 degrees and returns it to within 6 degrees of upright. A green lift flag, a post 8 mm square hidden inside the far end of the fork frame (away from the robot) with the forks down, rises out of the frame's top as the forks rise, 2 cm above it at full lift, so the lift shows from above. A red release pedal with a black ribbed plate 2 x 2.2 cm sticks out from the pump unit toward the robot, on an arm 5.2 cm long, its plate center 6.4 cm from the jack's center line and 2.4 cm above the floor; it is spring-returned up, and while it is held down 8.6 degrees or more (8 mm at the plate) the forks come down at 1 cm/s. A loaded pallet sits on the lowered forks, its center at x 28, y 9.8: a wooden single-deck stringer pallet 15 cm along the forks by 12.5 cm across (1,200 x 1,000 mm), with seven deck boards 2.4 mm thick on three stringers 4.8 mm wide and 1.43 cm tall, 1.67 cm tall in all, and on it a stretch-wrapped block of brown cartons with taped tops and white labels, 13 x 10.5 x 6 cm; 300 g in all (about 150 kg). The forks run between the stringers, their tops 3.7 mm below the deck, and the pallet's back is 2 mm from the fork frame. The bay is a rectangle of 1 cm yellow floor tape, flat on the floor, 15.5 cm (along x) by 18 cm (along y) inside, centered at x 28, y -7.2, 17 cm along the jack's travel from the pallet's start. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run and scores the end. The pallet rides clear when it sits on the forks (its center within 2 cm of its place on them) with its stringers' lowest point 1 mm (8 mm) off the floor, so the whole load is on the forks and none on the floor; two pump strokes leave it 2.4 mm up after the loaded forks' 1.1 mm sag, which counts. Two mistakes score 0 and are irreversible, each counted when it lasts 2 control steps (0.1 s). One is dragging the pallet on the floor with the forks down: before the first lift (the pallet carried clear 1 cm toward the bay) its footprint may shift 1.8 cm from its start, the 1.3 cm the pump strokes rock the jack and load in the scripted demo plus a 5 mm margin, and after it the slides of every set-down add up, never reset by a later lift, to at most 5 mm (4 cm at full size). The other is the pallet tipped past 15 degrees. Doing nothing, only pumping, or never carrying the pallet clear 3 cm closer to the bay (along the line from its start to the bay's center) also scores 0. Carried, but with a corner of the pallet's footprint past the middle of the bay's tape at the end, scores 0.25. In the bay with the forks not fully down scores 0.25: fully down means the pump's level back to 0, cross-checked with the fork joint within 1.5 mm (12 mm) of its bottom, and the pallet resting flat on its stringers (lowest corner within 2 mm of the floor, within 3 degrees of level). Forks down in the bay but the handle not upright (more than 7 degrees from vertical, past the zone its return spring holds), the pedal not let up (more than 6 degrees down), a gripper with closed fingers within 3 cm of the jack or the pallet, or either still moving (1 mm per step) scores 0.5. Finished scores 1.0 with both arms home and 0.9 with an arm not home; home means each tool point within 3 cm of where it started and still, so the aisle is clear. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial the 1 mm lift is too small for an overhead camera: film from the side at floor level (or slide a 1 mm feeler gauge under a stringer) to check the pallet is clear before the jack rolls, mark the pallet's start to measure any slide, then measure each corner against the tape, check the pallet rests on the table with the forks on their bottom stops, the handle within 7 degrees of vertical, the pedal up and the arms home.
reset_notes: Lower the forks fully, stand the handle upright and set the jack and the pallet back at their start, with the pallet's back 2 mm from the fork frame and centered across the forks. Nothing is used up.
fidelity: The model is at 1:8 scale with masses scaled by volume, and the pump is a modeled law, not hydraulics: each full handle stroke raises the forks 3.6 mm through a stiff joint drive, and the held pedal lowers them at 1 cm/s. The jack does not steer, its load rollers are low-friction spheres that slide rather than turn, the steer wheels roll with fixed resistance, the cartons are one rigid block, the table top stands in for the floor and the green lift flag is a camera marker.
